[OPINION][LISP] Why lisp is considered as powerful? And how Lisp status in current world?

I would define powerful in the context of Lisp as flexible. That's really the biggest strength of all the Lisps. The flexibility of Lisp comes from homoiconicity. In Lisp you write your program like this (define (add x y) (+ x y)) and the fundamental data structure of Lisp is the list, which is written similarly as (1 Y "A"). Homoiconicity means that a Lisp program is also a Lisp expression, you could take the source code any Lisp program and treat it as a Lisp expression and operate on that expression.

Lisp uses its homoiconicity for its famous macro system. A macro in Lisp is something that looks like a function call but instead of receiving a value receives the arguments as a Lisp expression. For example in Lisp you can define a macro if-zero like this: (defmacro (if-zero v then) `(if (= ,v 0) ,then ,v)

The backtick and commas are part of how you define a macro. This definition reads "replace (if-zero x y) with (if (= x 0) y x). Now the interesting bit is that with this macro you defined what would be syntax in another language. Only if the first argument is zero does the second argument get evaluated.

Macros allow even weirder stuff. Common Lisp for example has a famous super complex macro called loop. So with Lisp you can define your own language syntax based on what you need.

Now as for Lisp in the current world, I would say it's a niche language. Lisp is flexible but for most people it seems to be hard to read. The flexibility of defining your own syntax may be great but at the same time it is easy to overuse, leading to code that's hard to read since every expression may be a macro that turns it into a completely different thing.

Lisp has been extremely influential though and plenty of modern languages like Elixir and Rust have macro systems which are (ultimately) inspired by Lisp.
Wow so in simple terms, I can define syntax as I wish (in form of macro)? That'll cause a huge bloat and non-standarized syntax. It'll be hard to collaborate!

Pretty much, yes. Which is why Lisp culture strongly discourages unnecessary macros.

On the other hand it's pretty useful for defining domain specific languages. So in most languages with macros you tend to see experienced library writers define macros and most users only ever use them.

But don't underestimate the power of macros. In Go you don't have them and in effect that leads to people developing preprocessors just to avoid the repetitiveness of the language.
I'm not underestimating. In C# the syntax are locked. Without macros, it'll resort to many hacks just to modify the structure.
C# is a bit of an inbetweener with regards to macros. It doesn't have a true macro system but with expression trees you can operate on C# syntax and thus have something resembling run-time macros.
